---
title: "How we checked fasttrop"
description: >
  The comparisons with other implementations, the tests of the tuning and the
  bootstrap, and the simulations with a known effect.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
source("_setup.R")
val <- function(file) {
  utils::read.csv(system.file("validation", file, package = "fasttrop"))
}
```

::: {.key-points}
Key points

- On four small test panels with fixed tuning parameters, the ATTs of
  fasttrop and of the Python package `diff-diff` differ by at most 4e-8.
- The difference from the Python package of the authors is larger, but it is
  still less than 3e-5. It comes from the less accurate solver of that package.
- With each change to the code, 478 test expectations run on six platforms.
- With a block design and random selection of the treated units, TROP had an
  error 44% to 62% smaller than TWFE imputation.
- In a block-design simulation that selected treated units with large trends,
  TROP reduced the bias, but some bias stayed.
- In a staggered design with effects that differ between cohorts, a
  conventional TWFE regression had a bias of -0.36. TWFE imputation and TROP
  local had biases of -0.005 and -0.006.
- With parallel trends in a staggered design, TROP local had an RMSE 4% larger
  than TWFE imputation.
- With different trends in a staggered design, TROP local had a bias 20%
  smaller than TWFE imputation. But a large bias stayed.
:::

We checked fasttrop in three ways. First, we compared its results with other
implementations of TROP. Second, tests examine the tuning and the bootstrap.
Third, simulations with a known effect show how well the estimates and the
intervals work. They use a block design and a staggered design.

## Agreement with other implementations

When two independent programs give the same numbers, an error in one of them
is less likely. We compared fasttrop with two reference implementations at
fixed versions:

- The Python package `diff-diff` has the local method and the global method.
- The Python package `trop` from the authors of the paper has the global
  method for a block design.

The comparison used four small test panels and five sets of fixed tuning
parameters. The sets include TWFE imputation, weighted TWFE imputation, matrix
completion, and two sets for the full TROP estimator. One panel has a
staggered design, so it has no global estimate.

```{r agreement-fig, fig.asp = 0.42, fig.cap = "The absolute difference between the ATT of fasttrop and the ATT of each reference implementation. Each dot is one test panel with one set of tuning parameters. The axis has a log scale.", fig.alt = "A dot chart with a log scale from 1e-14 to 1e-4. For the local and global methods compared with diff-diff, all dots are below 1e-7. For the global method compared with the package of the authors, the dots go up to 2.5e-5."}
att <- val("oracle-att-comparison.csv")
att$comparison <- ifelse(att$reference == "trop", "Global method and the authors' package",
                         ifelse(att$method == "local", "Local method and diff-diff",
                                "Global method and diff-diff"))
att$comparison <- factor(att$comparison, levels = c("Global method and the authors' package",
                                                    "Global method and diff-diff",
                                                    "Local method and diff-diff"))
att$abs_diff <- pmax(abs(att$diff), 1e-16)
largest <- aggregate(abs_diff ~ comparison, data = att, FUN = max)

ggplot(att, aes(abs_diff, comparison)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = comparison == "Global method and the authors' package"),
             size = 2.8, alpha = 0.85, position = position_jitter(height = 0.12, seed = 1)) +
  geom_text(data = largest, aes(label = sprintf("largest %.1e", abs_diff)),
            hjust = 0.5, vjust = -1.6, size = 3.8, colour = ft_col[["ink"]]) +
  scale_x_log10(limits = c(1e-14, 1e-3), breaks = 10^seq(-14, -4, by = 2),
                labels = function(x) sprintf("1e%d", as.integer(round(log10(x)))),
                oob = scales::squish) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.5, 0.9))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ft_col[["coral"]], `FALSE` = ft_col[["teal"]]),
                      guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Absolute difference of the ATT (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

| Comparison | Largest difference |
|---|---|
| Local ATT, fasttrop and `diff-diff` | 4.0e-8 |
| Local effect for each cell, fasttrop and `diff-diff` | 1.1e-7 |
| Global ATT, fasttrop and `diff-diff` | 2.1e-8 |
| Global ATT, fasttrop and the authors' package | 2.5e-5 |
| Objective value with the same weights, relative to `diff-diff` | 7e-15 |

A difference of 4e-8 means that the two numbers agree in the first 7 decimal
places. The difference from the authors' package is equal to the difference
between the two reference implementations. The cause is the lower accuracy of
the conic solver in that package. Without the low-rank term, the difference is
3e-12 or less.

The last row of the table uses the same weights in both programs. Then both
programs find the same best fit, to the limit of the computer arithmetic.

## Tests of the tuning and the bootstrap

The test suite examines the parts of fasttrop that the comparison above does
not examine:

- The leave-one-out criterion does not use a cell in its own fit or in its own
  unit distances.
- The placebo criterion of the global method is the error of the placebo
  estimates.
- Each bootstrap draw is equal to a new estimate on the resampled panel.
  fasttrop keeps the selected tuning parameters fixed in each draw. Algorithm
  3 of the paper gives the resampling, but it does not say whether to select
  the tuning parameters again.
- The weights of the local method are equal to an independent R calculation
  of the formula in the paper.
- With `lambda = c(time = 0, unit = 0, nn = Inf)`, the result is equal to TWFE
  imputation.
- In a block design with no `NA` outcomes, TWFE imputation is equal to the
  result of a conventional TWFE regression. In a staggered design with effects
  that differ between cohorts, a test shows that the two results are
  different.
- The number of threads does not change the results. With a seed, the results
  are the same in each run.

The test suite has 478 expectations. GitHub Actions runs it with
`R CMD check --as-cran` on six platforms: Linux with four versions of R, macOS,
and Windows.

## Simulations with a known effect in a block design

A simulation makes many panels with a known effect. Then it measures how near
the estimates are to the truth. We used three simulations with a block design.
Simulations A and B have 200 panels each, and simulation A2 has 100 panels.

In each panel, the true effect is 1 for each treated cell. The untreated
outcomes have unit effects, period effects, a factor with a linear trend, a
second factor, and noise. All treated units start the treatment in the same
period.

| Simulation | Panels | Units | Treated units | Periods | Treated periods | Selection of the treated units |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 200 | 40 | 10 | 16 | 4 | A random draw |
| A2 | 100 | 80 | 30 | 12 | 3 | A random draw |
| B | 200 | 40 | 10 | 16 | 4 | A draw that favors the units with the largest trends |

We compared three estimators:

- TWFE imputation. In a block design with no `NA` outcomes, it gives the same
  estimate as a conventional TWFE regression.
- The local method of TROP, with the leave-one-out criterion on 80 sampled
  cells.
- The global method of TROP, with placebo cross-validation on 50 sets.

The tuning grid had four values for each parameter. All three estimators used
the same panels. The bootstrap used 200 draws for TWFE imputation and for the
global method, and 100 draws for the local method.

```{r sims}
sims <- rbind(val("known-truth-summary-A.csv"), val("known-truth-summary-A2.csv"),
              val("known-truth-summary-B.csv"))
sims$method <- factor(sims$method, levels = c("twfe", "local", "global"),
                      labels = c("TWFE imputation", "TROP local", "TROP global"))
sims$simulation <- factor(sims$design, levels = c("A", "A2", "B"),
                          labels = c("A: 10 of 40 units,\nrandom selection,\n200 panels",
                                     "A2: 30 of 80 units,\nrandom selection,\n100 panels",
                                     "B: 10 of 40 units,\nselection on the trend,\n200 panels"))
method_cols <- c("TWFE imputation" = ft_col[["coral"]], "TROP local" = ft_col[["teal_light"]],
                 "TROP global" = ft_col[["teal"]])
```

```{r rmse-fig, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "The root mean square error (RMSE) of each estimator in each simulation. A smaller RMSE is better.", fig.alt = "A bar chart in three panels. In simulation A, the RMSE is 0.75 for TWFE imputation, 0.30 for TROP local, and 0.29 for TROP global. In simulation A2, it is 0.31, 0.17, and 0.16. In simulation B, it is 1.37, 0.72, and 0.46."}
ggplot(sims, aes(method, rmse, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", rmse)), vjust = -0.5, size = 3.8) +
  facet_wrap(~simulation, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = method_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("TWFE\nimputation", "TROP\nlocal", "TROP\nglobal")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "RMSE") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.spacing = unit(1.2, "lines"),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 11, lineheight = 1.1))
```

With a random selection of the treated units (simulations A and A2), all three
estimators have small biases. The RMSE of TROP is 44% to 62% less than the
RMSE of TWFE imputation. Thus, on average, TROP gives estimates that are
nearer to the truth. In simulation A, the local method was nearer to the truth
than TWFE imputation in 170 of 200 panels.

In simulation B, the selection favors the units with the largest trends. TWFE
imputation has a large bias. TROP removes approximately half of this bias with
the local method and two thirds with the global method, but some bias stays.
The article [What TROP can and cannot do](limits.html) explains why.

```{r coverage-fig, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "The coverage of the 95% intervals: the share of panels in which the interval contains the true effect. The dashed line is the target of 95%. The bars show two Monte Carlo standard errors.", fig.alt = "A dot chart in three panels with the normal interval and the percentile interval for each estimator. In simulations A and A2, the coverage of TROP is between 0.89 and 0.99. In simulation B, the coverage is between 0.39 and 0.70 for all estimators."}
cov <- rbind(
  data.frame(sims[, c("simulation", "method")], interval = "Normal interval",
             coverage = sims$coverage_normal, se = sims$mc_se_normal),
  data.frame(sims[, c("simulation", "method")], interval = "Percentile interval",
             coverage = sims$coverage_percentile, se = sims$mc_se_percentile)
)
ggplot(cov, aes(coverage, method, colour = interval, shape = interval)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.95, linetype = "22", colour = ft_col[["muted"]]) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = coverage - 2 * se, xmax = pmin(coverage + 2 * se, 1)),
                 height = 0.2, position = position_dodge(width = 0.55)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.55)) +
  facet_wrap(~simulation, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Normal interval" = ft_col[["teal"]],
                                 "Percentile interval" = ft_col[["coral"]])) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Normal interval" = 16, "Percentile interval" = 17)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.3, 1), breaks = c(0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Coverage (the dashed line is 0.95)", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines"),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 11, lineheight = 1.1))
```

For TROP, the coverage of the normal interval is near 95% in simulations A and
A2. With 100 draws, the percentile interval of the local method has a coverage
of only 89% in simulation A. For this reason, the normal interval is the
default. In simulation A2, the global interval has a coverage of 99%, so it is
wider than necessary. In simulation B, the bias makes the coverage of all
intervals too low.

## Simulations with a staggered design

In a staggered design, the treated units start the treatment in different
periods. In this design, a conventional TWFE regression can give negative
weights to the effects in some treated cells.
[Hull (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39995) compares this regression with
two modern estimators in 1,346 specifications from 108 papers in ten economics
journals. One of the modern estimators is imputation. The study does not
examine TROP.

We made three simulations with a staggered design and a known effect.
Simulation C has one effect for all treated cells. Simulation D tests the
problem of the regression: effects that differ between cohorts. Simulation E
adds trends that differ between the cohorts.

These simulations do not repeat the study of Hull, because they use simulated
data. The theory of the paper is for a block design, so they do not test the
theory. They measure the bias, the error, and the coverage of the intervals.

```{r stag-data}
stag <- rbind(val("staggered-summary-C.csv"), val("staggered-summary-D.csv"),
              val("staggered-summary-E.csv"))
stag$method <- factor(stag$method, levels = c("twfe_regression", "twfe_imputation", "local"),
                      labels = c("TWFE regression", "TWFE imputation", "TROP local"))
stag$simulation <- factor(stag$design, levels = c("C", "D", "E"),
                          labels = c("C: one effect,\nparallel trends",
                                     "D: effects differ,\nparallel trends",
                                     "E: effects differ,\ntrends differ"))
stag_cols <- c("TWFE regression" = ft_col[["ink"]], "TWFE imputation" = ft_col[["coral"]],
               "TROP local" = ft_col[["teal"]])
sv <- function(design, method, col) stag[[col]][stag$design == design & stag$method == method]
sg <- function(design, method, col, digits = 2) {
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), sv(design, method, col))
}
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
stag_alt <- function(what, fmt) {
  parts <- vapply(c("C", "D", "E"), function(d) {
    values <- vapply(levels(stag$method), function(m) fmt(sv(d, m, what)), "")
    sprintf("In simulation %s, it is %s for TWFE regression, %s for TWFE imputation, and %s for TROP local.",
            d, values[1], values[2], values[3])
  }, "")
  paste(parts, collapse = " ")
}
alt_bias <- paste("A dot chart in three panels, one for each simulation. It shows the bias of each estimator.",
                  stag_alt("bias", function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)))
alt_coverage <- paste("A dot chart in three panels, one for each simulation. It shows the coverage of the",
                      "95% normal interval of each estimator. The target is 95%.",
                      stag_alt("coverage_normal", pct))

w <- val("staggered-twfe-weights.csv")
delta <- c("5" = 0.8, "8" = 0.6, "11" = 0.4, "14" = 0.2)
w$effect <- delta[as.character(w$cohort_start)] + 0.1 * w$periods_since_start
neg <- w[w$weight < 0, ]
weighted_mean <- sum(w$weight * w$effect) / sum(w$weight)
weight_bias <- weighted_mean - 1
trend_part <- sv("E", "TWFE regression", "bias") - weight_bias
less_e <- function(col) {
  round(100 * (1 - sv("E", "TROP local", col) / sv("E", "TWFE imputation", col)))
}
e_rows <- stag$design == "E" & stag$method != "TWFE regression"
e_cover_n <- round(stag$reps[1] * max(stag$coverage_normal[e_rows],
                                      stag$coverage_percentile[e_rows]))
others <- w$weight[w$cohort_start != min(w$cohort_start)]
alt_weights <- sprintf(paste("A bar chart in four panels, one for each cohort. For the cohort that",
                             "starts in period 5, the weight is %.1f in the first three periods and",
                             "%.2f in the last three periods. For the other cohorts, the weights are",
                             "between %.2f and %.2f. The dashed line is the weight 1 of TWFE",
                             "imputation."),
                       max(w$weight), min(w$weight), min(others), max(others))
```

Each panel has 60 units and 16 periods. Four cohorts of 12 units start the
treatment in periods 5, 8, 11, and 14, and stay treated. The 12 other units are
never treated. Thus, each panel has `r stag$cells[1]` treated cells. Each
simulation has `r stag$reps[1]` panels.

| Simulation | Effect in the treated cells | Trends of the untreated outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| C | 1 | Parallel |
| D | 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, or 0.2 for the four cohorts, plus 0.1 for each period since the start | Parallel |
| E | The same as in D | Different between the cohorts |

In simulations D and E, the effect is between `r min(w$effect)` and
`r max(w$effect)`. Its mean over the treated cells is `r mean(w$effect)`.
In each simulation, the truth is the mean of the effects in the treated cells.

In simulation E, the untreated outcomes also have the two factors of simulation
A. The score of a unit is its loading on the linear trend plus a random number.
The units with the largest scores start first. The 12 units with the smallest
scores are never treated. Thus, the trends of the cohorts differ.

We compared three estimators on the same panels:

- A conventional TWFE regression. It has unit effects, period effects, and one
  coefficient for the treatment. It uses all cells. Its standard error uses one
  cluster for each unit.
- TWFE imputation. It fits unit effects and period effects to the untreated
  cells. Then it takes the mean of the estimated effects in the treated cells.
- The local method of TROP. It has the same tuning grid and the same
  cross-validation as the simulations above.

In a block design with no `NA` outcomes, the regression and TWFE imputation
give the same estimate. In a staggered design, they can differ. The regression
gives its own weights to the treated cells. The two other estimators give the
weight 1 to each treated cell.

The global method is only for a block design, so we did not use it. The
bootstrap had 200 draws for TWFE imputation and 100 draws for the local method.
It kept the tuning parameters fixed. The regression has a normal interval only.

### The weights of the regression

With parallel trends, the regression estimates a weighted mean of the effects in
the treated cells. The weights depend only on the start periods of the cohorts.

```{r stag-weights, fig.asp = 0.6, fig.cap = "The weight of the regression on the treated cells. Each bar is one cohort in one period. The dashed line is the weight 1 of TWFE imputation. The mean weight is 1.", fig.alt = alt_weights}
w$cohort <- factor(w$cohort_start, levels = c(5, 8, 11, 14),
                   labels = paste("Cohort that starts in period", c(5, 8, 11, 14)))
w$sign <- factor(ifelse(w$weight < 0, "Negative weight", "Positive weight"),
                 levels = c("Positive weight", "Negative weight"))
ggplot(w, aes(period, weight, fill = sign)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ft_col[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "22", colour = ft_col[["muted"]]) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~cohort, nrow = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Positive weight" = ft_col[["teal"]],
                               "Negative weight" = ft_col[["coral"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(5, 8, 11, 14)) +
  labs(x = "Period", y = "Weight of the regression") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.spacing = unit(1.2, "lines"))
```

In `r nrow(neg)` of the `r nrow(w)` groups, the weight is negative. These are the
periods `r min(neg$period)` to `r max(neg$period)` of the cohort that starts in
period `r unique(neg$cohort_start)`. In simulations D and E, these cells have the
largest effects of the design. With these weights, the weighted mean of the
effects is `r sprintf("%.2f", weighted_mean)`, and the true mean is 1.

### The results

The table has the results. The bias has its Monte Carlo standard error in
parentheses. The column "SD" is the standard deviation of the estimates over the
panels, and "Mean SE" is the mean of the standard errors. The last two columns
are the coverage of the 95% intervals.

```{r stag-table}
tab <- data.frame(
  Simulation = as.character(stag$design),
  Estimator = as.character(stag$method),
  `Bias (MC SE)` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", stag$bias, stag$mc_se_bias),
  SD = sprintf("%.3f", stag$sd),
  `Mean SE` = sprintf("%.3f", stag$mean_se),
  RMSE = sprintf("%.3f", stag$rmse),
  `Normal interval` = pct(stag$coverage_normal),
  `Percentile interval` = ifelse(is.na(stag$coverage_percentile), "None",
                                 pct(stag$coverage_percentile)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
tab$Simulation[duplicated(tab$Simulation)] <- ""
knitr::kable(tab, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

```{r stag-bias-fig, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "The bias of each estimator. The number at the right of each row is the bias. The true effect is the mean of the effects in the treated cells. The bars show two Monte Carlo standard errors.", fig.alt = alt_bias}
lo <- min(stag$bias - 2 * stag$mc_se_bias)
hi <- max(stag$bias + 2 * stag$mc_se_bias)
span <- hi - lo
ggplot(stag, aes(bias, method, colour = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ft_col[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = bias - 2 * mc_se_bias, xmax = bias + 2 * mc_se_bias),
                 height = 0.25, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4) +
  geom_text(aes(x = hi + 0.07 * span, label = sprintf("%.2f", bias)),
            hjust = 0, size = 3.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~simulation, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = stag_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(lo - 0.04 * span, hi + 0.46 * span), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Bias", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.spacing = unit(2.2, "lines"),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 11, lineheight = 1.1))
```

In simulation C, the three estimators have small biases. Each bias is less than
two Monte Carlo standard errors from zero. The regression has the smallest
standard deviation. Its model is correct in simulation C, and it uses the
treated cells in the fit.

In simulation D, the bias of the regression is `r sg("D", "TWFE regression", "bias")`.
Thus, its mean estimate is `r pct(1 + sv("D", "TWFE regression", "bias"))` of the
true effect. Its 95% interval contains the truth in
`r round(sv("D", "TWFE regression", "coverage_normal") * stag$reps[1])` of the
`r stag$reps[1]` panels. TWFE imputation and the local method have the same
biases as in simulation C. They use only the untreated cells in the fit, and the
panels have the same noise in both simulations.

In simulation E, the biases of TWFE imputation and of the local method are
large. They are `r sg("E", "TWFE imputation", "bias")` and
`r sg("E", "TROP local", "bias")`, and the true effect is 1. The local method has
a bias `r less_e("bias")`% smaller and an RMSE `r less_e("rmse")`% smaller than
TWFE imputation. But the mean estimate of the local method is
`r sprintf("%.1f", 1 + sv("E", "TROP local", "bias"))` times the true effect.

In simulation E, the regression has the smallest bias,
`r sg("E", "TWFE regression", "bias")`. This result does not show an advantage of
the regression. Its bias has two parts. The weights give
`r sprintf("%.2f", weight_bias)`, as in simulation D. The different trends add
approximately `r sprintf("%.2f", trend_part)`. The two parts have opposite signs,
so they partly cancel, but in another design they can have the same sign.

```{r stag-coverage-fig, fig.asp = 0.5, fig.cap = "The coverage of the 95% intervals: the share of panels in which the interval contains the true effect. The dashed line is the target of 95%. The bars show two Monte Carlo standard errors.", fig.alt = alt_coverage}
cov <- rbind(
  data.frame(stag[, c("simulation", "method")], interval = "Normal interval",
             coverage = stag$coverage_normal, se = stag$mc_se_normal),
  data.frame(stag[, c("simulation", "method")], interval = "Percentile interval",
             coverage = stag$coverage_percentile, se = stag$mc_se_percentile)
)
cov <- cov[!is.na(cov$coverage), ]
ggplot(cov, aes(coverage, method, colour = interval, shape = interval)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.95, linetype = "22", colour = ft_col[["muted"]]) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = pmax(coverage - 2 * se, 0), xmax = pmin(coverage + 2 * se, 1)),
                 height = 0.2, position = position_dodge(width = 0.55)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.55)) +
  facet_wrap(~simulation, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Normal interval" = ft_col[["teal"]],
                                 "Percentile interval" = ft_col[["coral"]])) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Normal interval" = 16, "Percentile interval" = 17)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = c("0", "0.5", "1"),
                     expand = expansion(add = 0.04)) +
  labs(x = "Coverage (the dashed line is 0.95)", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.spacing = unit(2.2, "lines"),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 11, lineheight = 1.1))
```

In simulation D, the intervals of TWFE imputation and of the local method are
wider than necessary. The mean standard error of TWFE imputation is
`r sg("D", "TWFE imputation", "mean_se", 3)`, but the standard deviation of its
estimates is `r sg("D", "TWFE imputation", "sd", 3)`. The coverage of its normal
interval is `r pct(sv("D", "TWFE imputation", "coverage_normal"))`, and the
coverage of its percentile interval is
`r pct(sv("D", "TWFE imputation", "coverage_percentile"))`. The local method has
the same pattern.

We think that the bootstrap causes this result. It resamples the treated units,
so the number of units in each cohort changes in each draw. The effect differs
between the cohorts, so the mean effect also changes. Each simulated panel has
12 units in each cohort. We did not test this cause in a saved simulation.

In simulation E, the intervals of TWFE imputation and of the local method
contain the true effect in at most `r e_cover_n` of the `r stag$reps[1]` panels.
The bias is large compared with the standard deviation of the estimates, which
is `r sg("E", "TWFE imputation", "sd")` and `r sg("E", "TROP local", "sd")`. The
normal interval of the regression has a coverage of
`r pct(sv("E", "TWFE regression", "coverage_normal"))`.

These simulations have limits. They use one design with 60 units, 16 periods,
and four cohorts. They also use one tuning grid. The noise is independent
between the cells, but the noise in real panels can have correlation over time.

We did not test the other modern estimator of Hull. It averages the DiD
estimates of each cohort and period. We also did not compare TROP with a modern
estimator on real data. Hull recommends this comparison for each application.

## The scripts and the data

The package contains the scripts and the results, so you can run the checks
again. We ran the simulation scripts and the comparison scripts only on
Windows. GitHub Actions runs the test suite on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

- The folder `inst/validation` of the source package has the simulation
  scripts and the comparison report. In an installed package, use
  `system.file("validation", package = "fasttrop")` to find it.
- The folder `tests/testthat` has the test suite and the reference results.
- The script `data-raw/oracle_fixtures.py` in the GitHub repository made the
  reference results.
